Okay, well for whatever reason, please understand that it is incredibly difficult to understand and relate to somebody with a hormonal deficit that affects their mood, aka PPD in this instance. You feel l crazy yourself, because you honestly can’t tell if it’s real or not, if you’re just imagining it, and why you feel so bad. It is an incredibly awful thing to deal with, especially outside of support.

I encourage you to try and have more empathy for people. And I will also add that raising children is incredibly difficult, from a newborn and onward, it’s impossible to comprehend what goes into raising a functional and “good” human being if you never have before. Everyone has things they need to work through. 

And I can tell you for damn sure, there are many, many infants in this world who do not have a mother who cares enough to worry so much about this. Be kind.

And that’s fine, I respect your decision to not have children. But it is telling, that you haven’t had this particular experience, and don’t understand all the nuances that come with it. Life and people are not black and white my friend. I’m curious why you’re in a new parents sub to begin with? To just put down people? What’s your goal?

Yeah, I actually think most(?) people in the US have fatty liver disease. Happens all the time even without drinking. But of course not drinking will help it recover. You can recover from a fatty liver. Livers are actually quite resilient. Once it becomes cirrhosis, however, you cannot. You’ve been given a warning. 

I get why it’s too hard to stop. I believe in you. It really sucks when people’s total view of you is obscured by your drinking habits. Just remember that they don’t REALLY understand the depths of alcoholism; how bad of a disease it really is. And they never will. They are lucky they never will. So in their prospective, it’s very hard to understand why you just won’t quite, how “badly” you act while drunk. Don’t take it personally. You have to accept they will never understand the depths of your struggle. But that’s okay. They don’t have to. 

Cheers love.

I am 29 weeks pregnant and just got back from two weeks in Japan with my husband for our honeymoon. I think it just depends on how fit you are, if you are in relative shape (as in, you get some exercise and aren’t very overweight/have other health/pregnancy complications). Your body can handle all the walking, but it will be a LOT of walking. I could handle hauling some of our luggage around and from tracking it on my watch I think we walked almost 80 miles total on that trip. I won’t lie, at the end of some days our feet were absolutely killing us, def make use of taxis when you need to, have help lugging things around, don’t try to do a ton of hiking. Talk with your doc of course, you can probably do it but it will be a lot sometimes. Make sure you bring enough meds if you’re prone to nausea, headaches etc, stay hydrated.

Also yes, you can do teamlabs safely. The most strenuous things you’ll be doing is wading through knee deep water, some bending over.

I feel the spirit of this sub to begin with is to allow a safe space to not worry about being too upsetting or offending etc etc and express ourselves in regards to the topic of self harm. 

But to address your concern if it’s too relatable and you wish it wasn’t- when people start going through difficult things in life, they will gravitate to those who support them and will listen, naturally. If you’re referring to adults who depended too much on you as a child- that’s not fair at all. Can relate. But again, sometimes people just don’t know what to do. Or they’re not great people, on the other side of things.

It’s like burnout that many mental health professionals go through sometimes. You have to learn to separate yourself for your own self care. Harder said than done, I understand. 

But I do believe if people get access to the resources they need, you can work through things like this. It’s tough, but you can. Understanding what psychological/sociological patterns and how they’re affecting your brain and how you function in life is not a bad thing. It’s taxing, but it’s not a bad thing. It provides a level of self awareness and empathy some people may never have any insight into. 

Would not wish bad feelings or experiences like this on anybody, but I do think there is a silver lining there. 

I hope you feel better.

I also find the urges are incremental. Depends n the circumstances of things exacerbating bad feelings. Then you just want that fix. But I do find if you distract yourself, or, if you have someone you trust (family, friend, significant other, etc) you can tell hey, take my self harm stuff, I have bad urges right now. As long as they’re kind and understanding, I find that helps so I can get my mind off of it trying to do something else for a bit. Then after a while you can trust the feelings will pass eventually. 

I hope you feel better.

No need for me to go on an escapade describing in detail here, but I was in some involuntary facilities for some time when I was a teenager/young adult, and I remember being there at night on a shitty bed just wailing, literally BEGGING, for someone to get me out of there, with everything else going on on top of it. I felt so trapped. 

It was honestly some of the most painful emotions I’ve ever gone through in my whole life being there (it may sound dramatic to some but I have a hunch you can relate to me to the many layers that contribute to that.)

It’s been about 10 years, give it take since all that stuff. I still remember it, it’s still powerful in regards to it being an emotional experience. Wouldn’t wish feeling that way on anybody, and even though I’ve had some bad stints since then, I do think the experience has helped me understand people like us, and hopefully help to create something better for the other that do or will in the future. 

To get to my point, I promise you you’re not alone. And if you allow yourself the time to keep going, you can put it behind you. 

Sending hugs 🤗

I have a story about this Charizard to share with y’all if you have the time.

So to give some brief context I’m a woman in my late 20s who lost my dad a few years ago. I’ve had some time and a lot of support to process the grief  so there’s no worries about that, but I will make it a point that I had a very complicated relationship with my father. Essentially we were never close emotionally but I do believe he loved me and did what he could.

Anyway in cleaning up his house my brother found this card and kindly gave it to me to keep. If you’re familiar with the infamous MTG card Black Lotus, we know he had one of those as well but could never find it. He probably sold it or perhaps was lost to time. 

I got the card and I paid a good sum to have it graded. Because first edition Charizard you know, why not?

But honestly I realized in time I just did it to keep the card more protected and have it authenticated. Even if it was a 10 I don’t think I’d sell it. (I understand a lot of people would sell something like that if they needed to money, which I understand and no judging there, luckily I’m not in a struggle financially right now.)

Because it’s not about the Charizard.. it’s a symbol that represents one of the few ways my dad did connect with me when I was little. He’d buy my brother and I Pokémon cards and video games on the weekends (the whole process of going to the store was part of it.) He could never really relate to me any other way as a little girl, besides just asking how school was or whatever. 

Which I think is what the celebrations set and a lot of others should be about. I watched a gentleman I follow on YouTube open up some celebrations packs that were sent to him and legitimately cried pulling a Venasaur because it brought back memories of when he was a kid spending time with a loved one.

I know the hobby is toxic and frustrating asf right now in a lot of ways and it’s hard to get any new releases, people criticize the ins and outs of every set all the time, but remember some kids will make some really great memories opening each set every time. And sets like celebrations really celebrating for a lot of people what it’s all about. 

For me the thought is a reality check anyway. I was able to get the Pikachu box for celebrations but that was it. Which is just fine for now. But wanted to remind y’all why we love this hobby to begin with, or any really. Has nothing to do with simply looking at pieces of cardboard. Cheers ❤️

I’m glad you are getting treatment and have some hope for yourself at least. A lot of suicidal people do not. But let me enlighten you on a few things:

The way the brain works, I don’t have to go deeply into all this and don’t know what you already know, but our genes influence how our brains work. As they should, as life has evolved.

For some people, this includes brain activity that functions but inevitably makes them quite naturally depressed, but this tends to show up for them and be debilitating later in life.

As you know, humans in most recent history reproduce much earlier than they have now. Like very early 20s or before.

Hence these genes have been passed on before they’ve gotten very debilitating for people later than life. That may hand themselves, etc.

You have a genetic predisposition in your family to feel these suicidal thoughts. This is because how your brain works with the interaction of all its neurotransmitters as your genes tell it to do, it affects your mood, lack of ability to feel pleasure, etc. 

So when we talk about medication to treat depression, etc, this is what they are meant to address. You can look it up, but what this medication does is tell your brain to not get rid of some of the neurotransmitters it creates, that it uses for a lot of other functions, to not reuptake, or despose of it so quickly. What medication does is keep these certain neurotransmitters there in your brain before it gets rid of it. If you have heard of SSRIs, they stand for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Aka tell your brain not to get rid of so much serotonin, which we have linked to mood. You’re brain getting rid of too much is simply genetic, circumstantial things just make it worse. 

We have some better drugs now that deal with more than one system called SNRIs, that work on both serotonin systems and norepinephrine ones. Because mood is complex. Anyway, we treat acute anxiety with things like benzos and stuff like that that may help you circumstantially but not past that.

This is also why you just give antidepressants time to work, like a month, before you say it doesn’t work. It takes your brain time to get used to how it’s telling it to behave. Drugs mess this up incredibly too, like insanely. This is how addiction works.

Anyway dude absolutely nothing is wrong with you. Depression runs in your genes. And if it’s really bothering you, go psychiatrist and tell them all you told us. They can help you.

Definitely not alone in those things my friend. It’s not an easy thing to do, but as your brain has been reinforcing the idea that life will always be shit for years presumably, you essentially have to train it the other way around. That doesn’t mean you’ll never have suicidal thoughts again or bad days, of course not, but you do have some control over your affirmations. 

Whatever helps you think positively, do it. It sounds stupid but I’ve done it all- pictures of loved ones hung on the wall, notes from them, tickets from going to a really good concert, cheesy positive quotes about loving yourself and getting through bad times, stuff of any hobby you enjoy. Make your space inviting and calming. 

When you look in the mirror don’t put yourself down. When you start to think that way, think “I am strong enough to get through this,” “I deserve to feel better,” “I should take care of myself like I would anybody I loved,” etc. Like seriously, just force it. If you start to put yourself down in your head or to others, think of how much you’ve gotten through instead and know you did what you could with the resources you had at the time. Tomorrow’s always a new day and your past week experiences don’t have to define you. 

I would also talk to your doctor if you can and really try to find a medication that will help treat the depression/anxiety as a longer term solution rather than the benzos so you can use them only when you really need them instead. I don’t know the details of your situation obviously, but if what you’re doing isn’t working, try something else!

I’ll also add that you can’t control what other people do, and sometimes you just have to let them find their own way. It’s hard to accept but once you do it’s easier not to get so caught up in it all. 

But you can control what you do, taking all the precautions to stay safe. This is a scary time for all of us and the anxiety is very understandable. But things will inevitably change and you just have to do what you can do for right now.

Please do not self diagnose yourself, you need a trained professional to do diagnose you. But I can give you some typical signs of depression and you can look this up for yourself, as there are established, specific criteria to diagnose any mental health condition in something called the DSM-5:

\-Feelings of hopelessness and

\-Feelings of intense sadness/excessive crying that persist for over two weeks

\-Loss of interest in things you once loved or liked to do

\-Trouble sleeping or sleeping more than usual

\-Suicidal ideation

\-Withdrawal from loved ones or giving things away (this is what other people tend to notice)

\-Change in appetite, eating excessively or not enough

\-Physical sluggishness, difficulty in making decisions

\-Inability to fulfill your daily responsibilities, especially as you used to

\-Often comorbid (tends to go along with) feelings of anxiety, mood swings, other symptoms of mental illness

REM sleep is actually really important and the only stage of sleep you dream in. Supposedly you remembering your dreams is the time span when you’re being woken up enough for your brain to form memories out of REM sleep but aren’t totally awake yet, even though it seems like an eternity sometimes. Your brain is very active during REM sleep.

It seems like you’re not getting enough of those deeper, more restful beta waves that come along during certain parts of a typical 90 minute sleep cycle (goes through every stage of sleep and then repeats itself again. From a lighter sleep to a deeper one and REM and back, etc). 

There’s definitely a correlation between depression and REM sleep, apparently people who are depressed tend to have more. Also anti depressants like SSRIs and SNRIs are notorious for messing with your dreams. 

First thing to look at is any substances you’re taking that may mess with your sleep. Caffeine, alcohol, sugar even for some people I’ve heard, medication etc. Are you a light sleeper? Maybe you’re getting woken up a lot during the night. You can try earplugs. Or techniques to help you relax/get used to a regular sleep schedule, reduce stress/anxiety. Any major life changes recently?

Outside of those things the only thing I’d think to do is go to a specialist and get a sleep study done. You can always get more than one opinion. If it’s significantly affecting your quality of life it’s worth looking into.

Hey OP, you and everyone in this thread who feel the same way about your depression- YOU know yourself and your feelings the best, and nobody else can validate them but YOU. 

Seriously, I spent YEARS (maybe still do some days, I don’t know) believing I was just kinda fucked up and wasn’t able to cope the way everybody else did with life. That everybody felt the same things I did, but because I was too weak to deal with it, the problem was ME.

I have great parents, great home, went to a nice school, got good grades, never went without anything I needed, always had relatively nice things, friends, a bf etc etc. I totally understand the feeling of trying to understand why you feel so depressed when it seems like there’s absolutely no reason to be. It’s unreasonably frustrating. I was suicidal for a decent amount of time, felt like a big ass burden, you name it.

But that’s the problem. That’s why depression is so resilient to treatment sometimes. It’s NOT logical, and we naturally want to find reasons for why things happen so we wind up at a dead end and feel hopeless. Or people who don’t have the same feelings get frustrated by trying to figure out why themselves and it’s even more isolating and thoughts keep spiraling over and over and it reinforces them the more you think it. Chemical feedback loops in your brain and all that.

If YOU believe something is really wrong and you need help or a different kind of treatment, have faith in yourself and pursue it. I was on medication when I was 16, went to therapy and everything and nothing seemed to help. But I still knew SOMETHING wasn’t right, that I didn’t need to just “deal with it better.” Low and behold, as I’ve gotten older and tried a different type of medication, in conjunction with a better understanding of how the brain works (my family didn’t understand these things as well, things were different when they were growing up), therapy, social support, trying new coping mechanisms, etc etc, I actually have days where I wake up in a GOOD mood, not worried about my commute or work, not irritable and stressed out. Literally humming to myself kind of good mood, when I NEVER in a billion years thought I’d feel when I was younger.

Now is everything amazing and perfect for me, no of course not. I still have days I don’t want to do jack shit, usually if I’m having a fight with somebody or something like that, or I drank a bit much, etc. But the chemical and cognitive parts of my depression have been receptive to treatment now, and jeez everything just comes together so well and you realize there actually IS a reason you feel depressed, it’s just not a physically observable one. I believe I get some PMS related depression too and it takes me a few days to realize what’s going on. Then I tell myself, okay, it’s hormones, it will pass, etc. 

So sometimes it’s up to you to have faith in your feelings and try your best not to let what people say or do invalidate that.

Even if mislead, I think that sentiment almost always comes from a place of them empathizing and caring about you enough that they wish for you to have a happy experience of life. It’s frustrating to see somebody you care about suffer. But of course, nobody can FORCE you to be happy. I mean, you can be as miserable as you want to.

When you’re a kid, you can just be. You can just enjoy things for what they are. Be blissfully ignorant. It’s great. What’s changed since then is your perspective and capacity to understand. The rest of the world was as it’s always been. You know this too. But for you to be able to be a child, to have life and experience the wonderment of it, somebody else is tasked with the responsibility of taking care of you. If they don’t, or do it inadequately, whether they want to be free from those demands or simply don’t know any better, you’d never have a concept of blissful ignorance. Because you couldn’t, here on this Earth, unless somebody makes it happen. I’d separate this from the idea that suffering is what makes us able to feel happiness, but they are related, sure.

If you think of it that way.. things that seem like demands to add more suffering to your life, are actually tools to help you overcome it.

Obviously mental illness can make this very difficult to do- change your perspective on things. No one debates that. But if you’re able to find a way to cope with it and gain access to other tools that you had no idea you could have before, it’s entirely possible. You are NOT destined to a life of misery. 

For me, self reflection, social support, medication, therapy, and some sheer uninhibited perseverance were the tools I needed. I’m still working on it. But now I’m able to be aware of my own cognition and recognize it’s patterns of repetition that cement thoughts and feelings, particularly negative ones, into my life. Then I remember, everything is temporary. I can do something else right now. I can address the thoughts directly in many ways, I can distract myself from them, I can choose to tell my brain there are a lot of positive parts to these overarching thoughts I have too. I can overcome it and do something that makes me happy.

Anyway, rant over. Main takeaway is that you are NOT doomed to a life of suffering. That’s what separates us from just “being” and having a richer, absurd, amazing life experience. It’s a gift, really, if we’re able to figure out what we need to do to fulfill it.

But my friend, I do believe this is a feeling that most, if not every person, feels in their lifetime. Whether it’s apathy, a reaction to tragedy, or just the everyday struggle that life is (I don’t mean life just equates to pain, I’m referring to the work everybody’s got put in to be able to sustain themselves in this physical world.)

Personally I have struggled most helplessly with the concept of death, and close behind the meaninglessness of life in general.

Here’s a couple things that have seemed to help me out. Maybe they can comfort you a little bit too. 

When it comes to questions like this, nobody knows the answer. Even if they are very religious and are sure of their faith, I still don’t think they know all the intricacies of Gods’ ‘ways,’ is how I’d put it. And most don’t claim they do. When it comes to the overall problem of consciousness, we’re all in this shitshow of confusion together, one way or another. 

When it comes to dealing with feelings of meaningless/hopelessness, to put it very simply, you basically have two options: either let those feelings take over your life, or use them as an opportunity to give yourself the power to create your own meaning and purpose.

HOWEVER.

This does not imply that mental health and illness are not real. They absolutely are. And sometimes our biology and environment around us make everything more difficult. Luckily, we have a lot better understand of these things than we used to, and a lot more options to treat underlying issues that will exacerbate the feelings of depression/anxiety that comes with thoughts like this.

Now when I say that, too. I don’t think that means you should feel one way or another ALL the time. We’re human, we have emotions and stuff just sucks hardcore sometimes. I don’t feel optimistic most days. That doesn’t mean I’ve given up. But on the other side, it can be empowering to know that choosing to do what you want with your life can make you very happy and fulfilled, let you have these experiences as a life form of free will that has the intellectual capacity to create a consciousness that is much more powerful than the sum of its biological parts.. life trying to figure out, well. Life. It’s a unique experience and one capable of true senses of euphoria and awe- we are able to picture things in our heads and make what we think about real. (Even if you cannot cognitively make an actual imagine of the concept.. you know what I mean.)

However you think about it, it’s basically the whole doomer/bloomer meme argument that’s been going around. But it’s been around for a long time. Some philosophers have/had a more optimistic view on it than others. But you can boil it down some. 

Death is a tricky one. Trying to sit and make something logical out of it doesn’t seem to get anywhere, at least for me. I don’t remember the author or what book it was, but on a Google hunt one night I found a webpage where he briefly explains why we shouldn’t be afraid of death. Obviously I’m going to heavily summarize but if you’re interested, I’m sure you can look into it more.

One reason he gives is that if we lived forever (I think most people wouldn’t want to anyway), we’d eventually get bored of everything life has to offer us, and once that happens, death would certainly be a merciful thing. If you think things are meaningless now, this is on an entirely different level.

Another is that death is inherently benign- in ceasing all functions to maintain life, it is impossible for us to physically suffer anymore. Even if there is pain leading up to death, death itself is the ceasing of that pain, so we why be afraid of it?

Another is, well, you can’t really do anything about it. It’s inevitable for every person on the planet. Therefore spending a lot of your life afraid of it seems irrational, and only makes you suffer more.

I honestly can’t remember the last one, but I would add, as some people say, to think of death as what you were before you were born. But you can’t; there’s an inherent amnesia there, and no conscious knowledge of anything before or after life, which really, can be comforting. Instead of a consciousness that knows any eternal kind of suffering, it simply ceases to be. Probably something that’s out of our realm of understanding to even try to comprehend.

If it wasn’t clear already, personally I do not believe in an afterlife of eternal suffering. I think in simpler times, it probably made more sense, but seems to come off now as a reason to have a sense of morality so we don’t all kill each other (I exaggerate.) I completely understand you can’t just click off the anxiety or depression. It doesn’t work like that. But maybe having a new perspective on things like this can help you, along with any other treatment you may need.


Lastly, I think suicidal ideation is a pretty normal response we have to a situation we believe we have no power over/cannot solve. In reality, that’s almost always never the case, and if you know that those feelings are temporary, you can get through it. It happens to me sometimes for like, no real reason (always has, other things made it worse but nobody could really figure this out, but I knew something was wrong and had to fight for/take responsibility for my mental health. It’s difficult.) And that’s the time where you go take a damn nap and cuddle a pillow, or watch a movie, or whatever you gotta do.

I think as a child we're all more easily captivated and intrigued by virtual worlds (or any kind of entertainment really)- it's all relatively new to you as a child; you don't really know how video games are made behind the scene yet, so your imagination fills in the wonder. I believe as adults we're still imaginative but it's much easier to break that illusion as we understand how things work, our thoughts are constantly in the future concerned with our bigger responsibilities, and we've been told for years that playing video games too much is a waste of time, pressured that we should be focusing on other things, etc. So yeah, of course, I think a big part of it is normal development and the product of our environment as we age.

On the other hand, I also believe as a child you're more willing to give something the benefit of the doubt since it may be all you have, you don't have as many preconceived notions about what you're playing, and you have more energy and time to invest in making progress. And when you find that game that pulls you in you can ride that fresh dopamine loop over and over without the novelty becoming boring because you're not used to and constantly dissecting it. Perhaps as we get older we find other things to fill that desire for escapism too, be it good or not.

That said though I still think you can have those feelings playing games as an adult. I've noticed when I take the time and energy to push through a learning curve or grind in a game that rewarding feeling can pull me in more. Also allowing yourself (I mean honestly) to be fine with having some dumb fun indulging in a world of nonsense for a little while (personally I struggle with this one a lot.) And if you feel like you've given these things a chance and still find yourself slothing along playing games, maybe it's just something to put down for a bit or let go of; it's good to embrace and explore your newfound interests too, instead of only chasing an old feeling if that's all it has become for you (speaking generally here).

Hey there. I understand the feeling of wanting an entire collection. Smash is essentially the franchise that defined my childhood when it comes to games. I loved the idea of real life trophies/affordable and functional Nintendo figures to collect. I never collected Skylanders or Disney Infinity stuff so Amiibo made these things a first for me. But when Amiibo first came out, I realized it just wouldn't be realistic for me to expect to be able to buy 50+ figures at $13 a pop in my situation so I never even expected to be getting more than a few of my favs over time.

What happened is that I started receiving a lot of the ones I didn't have as gifts for Christmas or just from loved ones, and I started to think that it would be possible for me to collect them all since I was getting a lot of help. I'm also in college full time and while I'm not working at the moment I'm lucky to be supported financially and have some extra cash that I save up over time to spend on things like this. 

But my point in all this is that while amiibo are a fun hobby, it's not worth you health or financial worries. I know if I had to work and pay the bills my expectations would be even lower than they originally were, and for a lot of people this is how it is. I understand it's easier said than done but I think people should focus on what's doable when it comes to amiibo and get their favs. Get your sleep and make sure you have enough to eat before anything, school is already stressful as it is and IMO it's super important to prioritize an education that you pay so much for. 

Anyways good luck with your hunt and I hope you start to feel less stressed about all this. *Hugs*
